Review – Moa “Southern Alps”

They call it a “White IPA”. Brewed using Nelson Sauvin and citra and fermented using Belgian ale yeast and coriander.

Aroma:

I made the mistake of trying this one straight out of the fridge, which didn’t do it justice initially. After letting it warm up the hop profiles came through and the “IPA” character was evident on the nose. The Belgian yeast gives it the typically spicy aroma which reminded me of Leffe Blonde

Taste:

The Belgian character is at the front and I would classify this as a Belgian ale first and foremost, which was actually a pleasant surprise for me as I had picked it up looking for an IPA flavour. The NZ hops are not overpowering in this and it lets the yeast and high alcohol content do the talking. After a pint I was eager for another right away, which is pretty much the best outcome you can have for a new beer. Being bottle conditioned I made sure to swirl the last dregs into my glass (cloudy beer never scares me), which I would recommend doing.

Avaliability:

In New Zealand pretty much everywhere, I picked it up in New World but I know Pak’n’Save carry it as well and at a good price. The recent sales problems for Moa are being reflected in some good priced beer from them and I will be working my way through their range.

I tried searching online for both UK and USA stockists, no joy. This isn’t Moa’s standard range but strangely no Moa beer showed up in my searches, which is odd as they are a larger player in the New Zealand beer scene. If anyone does know where to pick it up internationally please let me know.

I feel the urge to clear up some common misconceptions about all this..

For the past 5-6 years, the EU has lent Greece bailout money along with the requirement that they force ever harshening austerity measures on its country. Austerity simply has never worked before historically to dig a country out of debt/depression, has not been working in Greece, and won't work in the future. This is why the situation has gotten worse over time.

Last Sunday the Greeks voted against EU bailout money, but now Tsipras is bargaining with the EU for a bailout of around 50 B euros. These conditions are harsher than ever, and are humiliating to Greece. This is widely seen as a sign from Germany that they want to kick Greece out of the eurozone.

Let's look at history. After WW1 the Allies demanded every cent in repatriation to be paid back by the Germans. This caused the weak German economy to collapse, enter hyperinflation, and depression. After WW2 the Allies learned their lesson; they forgave German debts and loaned them money. This lead to the German economy prospering in the 1950's.

What they EU should do is forgive Greek debts ideally, if not that loan Greece money without austerity measures. What Greece should do is develop a plan to exit the euro, which is a huge financial catastrophe, as it doesn't allow each country to alter inflation/deflation rates at their will. The consequences of this inability is most profound during a financial recession, like in 2008-09.

The problem is, the EU doesn't trust Greece to repay anything. Not their current debt, not a new loan without austerity measures. I think Germany knew Greece wouldn't like current proposed measures, and actually want a less harsh than currently proposed deal. It appears that's whats going to happen. Greece needs the money.

I don't think you should expect to learn every single command. The ones you use often you'll start remembering, the ones you seldom use you'll have to keep looking up. There's nothing wrong with that.

I'm not sure why you need to go to forum to ask questions, usually Google will find the answers for you (possibly in a forum).

Don't get discouraged, you just have to get through the initial phase where you don't know anything at all.

You gotta start somewhere man. Hopefully the sites you're getting these commands from are explaining exactly what they do, which is most important. Just going over other people's commands and figuring out what each part does is the best way to learn in my opinion.http://www.commandlinefu.com is one of my favorite places to just poke around and see what people have come up with.

Over time, once you've memorized a bunch of commands, you'll run into a situation where you'll need to combine two of the commands you already know, or you'll have to tweak a command you have saved in a text file to do something a bit different.

This is something that takes years of serious work in order to just pull your own complicated commands out of thin air, but like I said the more you understand what each bit of the command does, the more you'll be able to modify their commands and create your own.

Hope this helps.

Another thing about Linux is that there's never just one way to do something, so you always have options on how to accomplish a task. For example, I usually just dd from /dev/zero to a hard disk instead of using fdisk to delete the MBR just out of habit. Trying to find as many solutions to a specific problem will also give you a better idea of what is going on, which will help you come up with your own commands in the future.

For example, I usually just dd from /dev/zero to a hard disk instead of using fdisk to delete the MBR just out of habit.

Using dd is probably more secure anyway, since it renders the contents unrecoverable. Personally, I normally use wipefs, since it's more general than fdisk and much faster.

Keep googling. The first step is figuring what programs/commands/tools you can use in different situations, the second step is figuring out how to use them in different situations. There is no shortcut to retaining obscure text commands. The more you use the command line the more familiar you will become with using it - just keep using it and keep googling situations as they come up. Eventually you will think "ah, I don't have to google this one, I can just use xxxx" You will then use xxxx incorrectly and either get an error or results that you did not expect - then you will google and find out what you did wrong. Then one day you will realize that you have been reading man pages for three hours and you are currently nine pages into a topic that is in no way related to what you initially wanted to do.
Googling isn't bad, but you shouldn't be just copy-pasting commands found on the internet. Always check the actual meaning (man foobar and foobar --help). We remember what we understand.
Not sure if you mostly copy and paste the commands you find online but if you are I would suggest typing them in as you'll commit them to memory more effectively.

IMO, if you want to learn to use the terminal, you won't learn until you HAVE to use the terminal.

Try to install one of the distros that require you to use the terminal to install it. Try Gentoo, Funtoo, or LFS. I suggest having a PC or your phone next to you for instructions, but installing and using these distros will help you learn.

I learned a LOT about the inner workings and the command line by installing Gentoo in 2002. I had a working knowledge of Linux, but nothing like that.

You won't learn everything, but you will learn enough to manage your system and get around after the first install.

Once you get the basics down and even before LFS has some neat shortcuts in their book. To master the basics, its like typing. You have to practice and find a style that suits you. As others have said, it will become muscle memory over time. You didn't learn english overnight, and you won't learn the shell overnight either. The shell is a language, much english; it provides a highly detailed, efficient, concise, and unambiguous to communicate ideas to the computer, and that means it is also obtuse, complex, and not always intuitive.

Once you've been at it for a while, you won't think about it anymore. I imagine that when you speak english, you don't think about vocabulary and word-choice before expressing an idea, it just comes naturally and you speak. In the same way, someone experienced with the shell does not think in commands, they think in ideas an concepts, the commands just come naturally without thinking.

To emphasize the point again, this type of muscle memory does not happen overnight, it takes repetition. The best way to get in that repetition is to do everything you possibly can via the shell, at least until you get to a skill level you are happy with. That means partitioning, file management, file editing, word processing, programming, changing settings, and so on. Then, once you are comfortable doing those things via the shell you can start to work GUI tools back in where they make you faster or more efficient.

Use 'whatis'

grep [] (1) - print lines matching a pattern
$ whatis pidof

To get started, go into /bin or /usr/bin, at run `whatis' on some of them. If it sounds useful, open the man page.

Something i figured a while ago that may be useful: 

$ cd /bin; whatis * | more

That will tell you what everything does in /bin. Use that information along with manual pages.

Use the manual. I don't mean that to be a dick, and it sounds like an Arch purist thing, but I'm serious.

If you need a Terminal command, and you're not sure exactly what it is, you can use man -k [search-term] and it'll give you an output for manuals that mention your search-term. For instance, if your want to look for your mail message manager, your would:

$ man -k mail

savd (8) - control, logging and email alerting daemon

CURLOPT_MAIL_AUTH (3) - SMTP authentication address

CURLOPT_MAIL_FROM (3) - SMTP sender address

CURLOPT_MAIL_RCPT (3) - list of SMTP mail recipients

git-am (1) - Apply a series of patches from a mailbox

git-check-mailmap (1) - Show canonical names and email addresses of contacts

git-format-patch (1) - Prepare patches for e-mail submission

git-mailinfo (1) - Extracts patch and authorship from a single e-mail message

git-mailsplit (1) - Simple UNIX mbox splitter program

git-send-email (1) - Send a collection of patches as emails

gnutls_openpgp_crt_check_email (3) - API function

gnutls_x509_crt_check_email (3) - API function

gpgparsemail (1) - Parse a mail message into an annotated format

logrotate (8) - rotates, compresses, and mails system logs

logrotate.conf (5) - rotates, compresses, and mails system logs

mail (1) - send and receive Internet mail

mailaddr (7) - mail addressing description

mailx (1) - send and receive Internet mail

mailx (1p) - process messages

Net::SMTP (3perl) - Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Client

pam_mail (8) - Inform about available mail

perlfaq9 (1perl) - Web, Email and Networking

X509_check_email (3ssl) - X.509 certificate matching

X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_email (3ssl) - X509 verification parameters

xdg-email (1) - command line tool for sending mail using the user's preferred e-mail composer

Here, you get a comprehensive list of commands that incorporate your "mail" in some way. Since you're new, I'd stay away from items above level 1 or 2... which is the number in parentheses.

Once you find the command that you believe is what you're looking for, you can look up its individual manual. For instance, let's say you want the manual for the mail program, and learn what the command line functions are for that. You'd just use:

$ man mail

This will output the manual for the mail program. The manual is a WEALTH of information for every installed program you have installed, and can be a little intimidating. If you are having a hard time understanding the manual and how it works, you can actually pull up the manual on the manual! It's my favorite command, since it's:

$ man man

This will explain how the manual works, and how to read each one. It also explains the man -k function and how to use that in better detail.
